questions.q: Trace a bite of chapati from the mouth to the stomach. Name the parts that act on it and say what each does.
questions.a: Teeth crush and chew it. Saliva moistens it and changes starch to sugar; the tongue mixes it with saliva and pushes it into the food pipe. The food pipe's walls contract and relax in waves and push it to the stomach.
s: Teeth and saliva in the mouth
Food pipe wave movement to the stomach

questions.q: Define digestion and name the tube in which most of it takes place.
questions.a: Digestion is the breaking down of complex food components into simpler forms. It takes place in the alimentary canal.
s: Defines digestion as breaking complex food into simpler forms

questions.q: In which part of the human body does the digestion of food begin?
questions.a: The mouth

questions.q: Justify the advice 'chew your food well before swallowing' using three points about what happens in the mouth.
questions.a: Chewing crushes food into fine pieces (mechanical digestion). Longer chewing gives saliva more time to break starch into sugar, as chapati turns sweet when chewed for long. Saliva moistens the food and the tongue pushes it into the food pipe, so it is soft and easy to swallow. So well-chewed food is ready for the rest of its journey.
s: Saliva acts on starch for longer
Moistened, soft food is easy to swallow
Concludes by linking to the rest of the journey

questions.q:
(a) State two things saliva does to chewed food.
(b) Which organ mixes the chewed food with saliva?
questions.a: (a) It moistens the food, making it soft and easy to swallow, and its digestive juice breaks starch into sugar. (b) The tongue.
s: Part (a): moistens and acts on starch

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about digestion in the mouth and food pipe.
Statement 1: Digestion of food begins in the stomach.
Statement 2: The alimentary canal is a long tube that starts at the mouth and ends at the anus.
Statement 3: Saliva contains a digestive juice that acts on starch.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In Activity 9.1 the chewed rice in test tube B shows little or no blue-black colour with iodine.
Reason (R): Saliva contains a digestive juice that breaks starch into sugar.
questions.a: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Arjun, 12, brushes his teeth twice a day but does not clean his tongue or rinse his mouth after meals. He says, 'Brushing is enough, so the rest is extra.' His dentist asks him to check this against the advice in his science book.
(a) Name the first part of the alimentary canal where digestion begins.
(b) Which two habits from the book's advice does Arjun leave out, and what do they prevent?
(c) At 4 pm a friend gives him a sticky sweet and there is only a tap nearby, no brush. Decide what he should do and say why.
questions.a: (a) The mouth. (b) Cleaning the tongue and rinsing the mouth with water after each meal; they prevent tooth decay and bad smell. (c) He should rinse his mouth with water, as the book advises rinsing after eating; this helps prevent tooth decay and bad smell.
s: Part (b): tongue cleaning, rinsing, what they prevent
Part (c): rinse with water, reason from the book

questions.q:
Kavya's class repeats the rice and iodine activity. Four groups chew boiled rice for different times before adding the same amount of iodine. Group A does not chew, group B chews for 15 s, group C for 30 s and group D for 60 s. Colours seen: A deep blue-black, B medium, C light, D very faint.
(a) What does the deep blue-black colour of group A tell you about its rice?
(b) What trend do the colours show and what does it say about saliva?
(c) Predict the colour for a group chewing 90 s and say why the prediction needs a test.
(d) The class must advise Class 5 on chewing a mouthful of rice for 15 s or 60 s. Choose using the data, and name one thing these four tubes cannot tell you.
questions.a: (a) Starch is present in the rice, since iodine gives blue-black with starch. (b) Longer chewing gives lighter colour, so saliva breaks more starch into sugar with time. (c) Probably fainter or colourless, but it must be repeated to find out. (d) Advise 60 s as it leaves the least starch; the tubes cannot tell what happens to proteins and fats or in later parts of the canal.
s: Part (c): prediction with reason to test
Part (d): choice with limit of the data

questions.q: A teacher shows two tubes after adding iodine: tube P is deep blue-black and tube Q is almost colourless. Describe a set-up using boiled rice that would give exactly these observations, and explain tube Q.
questions.a: P: boiled rice taken directly with water. Q: boiled rice chewed for 30 to 60 seconds, then put in the same amount of water. Equal water and 3-4 drops of iodine in both. In Q saliva has broken starch into sugar, so little colour.
s: Tube P: unchewed rice with water
Tube Q: chewed rice, same water and iodine drops
Explains Q: saliva acted on starch

questions.q: Two test tubes hold equal amounts of rice and water. Tube X has boiled rice, tube Y has boiled rice chewed for a minute. After iodine drops, X turns deep blue-black and Y stays very faint. Which idea explains tube Y?
questions.a: Saliva broke down most of the starch into sugars
o: Saliva broke down most of the starch into sugars
Chewing only crushed the rice, which removed the starch
Saliva made the iodine solution too dilute to show colour
Chewing changed the starch into protein

questions.q: Aman says: 'Tube B shows no blue-black colour with iodine, so the saliva has made the starch of the rice vanish.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. Iodine only shows whether starch is present. In tube B the starch has not vanished; saliva has broken it down into sugar, which iodine does not turn blue-black.
s: Iodine shows only the presence of starch
Starch broken down into sugar, not vanished

questions.q: Differentiate between mechanical digestion and the action of saliva on food, giving one point for each.
questions.a: Mechanical digestion is done by teeth, which crush and chew food into fine pieces without changing what the food is made of. Saliva contains a digestive juice that changes starch into sugar.
s: Mechanical digestion: teeth crush and chew into pieces
Saliva: digestive juice changes starch into sugar

questions.q: Which statement about saliva is NOT correct?
questions.a: It breaks down the proteins of the food completely in the mouth
o: It breaks down the proteins of the food completely in the mouth
It moistens the food so that it is easy to swallow
It contains a digestive juice that acts on starch
More of it is released when we recall a favourite food

questions.q:
Match each part in Column I with its work in Column II.
Column I: 1. Teeth  2. Saliva  3. Tongue  4. Food pipe
Column II: A. mixes chewed food with saliva and pushes it towards the food pipe  B. crush and chew food into fine pieces  C. its digestive juice breaks starch into sugar  D. walls contract and relax in waves to push food to the stomach

Kavya wants to find out whether chewing for longer leaves less starch in rice. Plan an investigation: say what you will change, what you will keep the same, what you will observe, and what result would support the idea.
questions.a: Change: the time of chewing, for example 15 s, 30 s and 60 s. Keep same: amount of boiled rice, amount of water and number of drops of iodine. Observe: colour after adding iodine. Supporting result: the longer the chewing, the lighter the blue-black colour, because saliva has broken more starch into sugar.
s: Reason from the action of saliva on starch

questions.q:
(a) Name the tube that carries chewed food from the mouth to the stomach.
(b) Describe how its walls move the food along.
questions.a: (a) The food pipe (oesophagus). (b) Its walls contract and relax in a wave-like motion, pushing the food down to the stomach.

questions.q: Rohan chews a piece of plain chapati for a full minute and finds it turning sweet. His friend swallows his piece after two chews and notices no sweetness. What is the best explanation?
questions.a: Longer chewing gives saliva more time to change starch into sugar
o: Longer chewing gives saliva more time to change starch into sugar
The friend's chapati had no starch in it
Sweetness is produced by the teeth when they crush the chapati
The friend's saliva stopped being released after two chews

questions.q: Teeth crush and chew food into fine pieces. What is this initial breakdown of food called?
questions.a: Mechanical digestion

questions.q: Ananya's grandmother tells her to brush twice a day, clean her tongue and rinse her mouth with water after every meal. Give two reasons from your book why this is important.
questions.a: It prevents tooth decay and it prevents bad smell in the mouth.
s: Prevents bad smell in the mouth

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the small intestine.
Statement 1: The small intestine receives secretions from its own lining, the liver and the pancreas.
Statement 2: Bile is mildly basic and pancreatic juice is also basic.
Statement 3: Digested nutrients pass into the blood in the walls of the small intestine.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Ananya, 13, is diagnosed with celiac disease. Her doctor says gluten damages the inner lining of her small intestine and asks her to avoid foods that contain it. Her mother replaces wheat chapati in her tiffin with other foods. The canteen offers wheat sandwich, bajra roti, rye bread and jowar upma.
(a) Which function of the small intestine is lost when its lining is damaged?
(b) Why would Ananya feel weak even if she eats a full meal?
(c) Which canteen items contain gluten, according to your book?
(d) Decide which two items Ananya may take and justify the choice.
questions.a: (a) Absorption of nutrients. (b) Digested nutrients cannot pass into the blood properly, so energy and growth materials do not reach the body. (c) Wheat sandwich and rye bread, as gluten is in wheat, barley and rye. (d) Bajra roti and jowar upma, as millets such as jowar and bajra are naturally gluten-free.
s: Part (b): nutrients not reaching the blood
Part (d): bajra roti, jowar upma with reason

questions.q: Rohan says: 'All the digestion of proteins, carbohydrates and fats is finished in the stomach.' Is he right? Support your answer with the work of the stomach and of the small intestine.
questions.a: No. The stomach's juice breaks down only proteins. Pancreatic juice acts on carbohydrates, proteins and fats, bile helps fats, and the intestine's own juice further breaks fats, proteins and partly digested carbohydrates. Digestion therefore continues in the small intestine.
s: Small intestine and its secretions complete digestion

questions.q: Which part of the alimentary canal is the longest, at almost 6 metres?
questions.a: The small intestine

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT done by the secretions of the stomach?
questions.a: Breaking fats into tiny droplets

questions.q: Describe what happens to food in the stomach, in three points.
questions.a: The walls contract and relax to churn the food. It mixes with the secretion of digestive juice, acid and mucus, which break down proteins, kill harmful bacteria and protect the lining. The food becomes a semi-liquid mass.

questions.q: Define absorption of nutrients and name the part where most of it happens.
questions.a: Absorption is the passing of digested nutrients into the blood in the blood vessels in the walls of the small intestine. Most of it happens in the small intestine.

questions.q: Compare the stomach and the small intestine on what secretions reach the food, which food components they act on, what the food is like after the stomach, and where nutrients pass into the blood.
questions.a: Stomach: digestive juice, acid and mucus; acts on proteins; food becomes a semi-liquid mass; no absorption is described there. Small intestine: secretions from its lining, liver and pancreas; acts on fats, proteins and carbohydrates; nutrients pass into blood through its walls by absorption.
s: Stomach secretions and action on proteins
Small intestine secretions from three sources
Absorption into the blood only described for small intestine

questions.q: Give two functions of the acid in the stomach's secretion.
questions.a: It helps the stomach's digestive juice to break down proteins and it kills many harmful bacteria.

questions.q:
Match each source in Column I with the secretion or action in Column II.
Column I: 1. Liver  2. Pancreas  3. Lining of the stomach  4. Wall of the small intestine
Column II: A. bile that neutralises acids and breaks fats into droplets  B. pancreatic juice acting on carbohydrates, proteins and fats  C. digestive juice, acid and mucus  D. further breaks down fats, proteins and partly digested carbohydrates
Describe the three sources of secretions of the small intestine, saying what each does, and then say how digested nutrients leave the small intestine.
questions.a: The inner lining of the small intestine secretes juice that breaks down fats, proteins and partly digested carbohydrates. The liver secretes bile, which neutralises acids and breaks fats into droplets. The pancreas secretes basic pancreatic juice that neutralises acids and breaks down carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Nutrients pass into the blood in the wall by absorption.
s: Lining of the intestine and its action

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The acid in the stomach kills many harmful bacteria.
Reason (R): Mucus protects the stomach lining from the acid.
questions.a: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Mina swallows a piece of paneer (a protein-rich food). Name the secretions that act on its protein on the way, in order, and say where each is made.
questions.a: First the digestive juice of the stomach (with acid, made by the stomach lining). Then pancreatic juice made by the pancreas. Then the digestive juice from the wall of the small intestine.
s: Juice from the small intestine wall

questions.q: Differentiate between digestion and absorption with one point each.
questions.a: Digestion is breaking complex food into simpler forms by digestive juices. Absorption is the passing of the simpler digested nutrients into the blood through the walls of the small intestine.

questions.q:
After a meal of dal, rice and ghee, Dr Mehta studies three patients. Patient P makes very little acid in the stomach. Patient Q's liver makes very little bile. Patient R's pancreas does not secrete pancreatic juice.
(a) What are two things P's stomach is less able to do?
(b) What two jobs of bile are reduced in Q?
(c) Why does R's problem cover the widest range of food components?
(d) Q may be given either a low-fat meal or a low-starch meal tomorrow. Choose one and say why, and why Q still has some fat digestion.
questions.a: (a) Help break down proteins and kill many harmful bacteria. (b) Neutralising acids from the stomach and breaking fats into tiny droplets. (c) Pancreatic juice acts on carbohydrates, proteins and fats. (d) Low-fat, as bile helps break fats into droplets; Q still has some fat digestion because pancreatic juice and the juice of the intestinal wall also act on fats.
s: Part (a): protein breakdown and killing bacteria
Part (b): neutralising acid and fat droplets
Part (d): low-fat with two other juices acting on fats

questions.q: After an operation, a man's liver can no longer secrete bile. Which problem would you expect first?
questions.a: Fats are not broken into tiny droplets, so their digestion is harder
o: Fats are not broken into tiny droplets, so their digestion is harder
Proteins are no longer broken down in the stomach
Starch is no longer changed to sugar by saliva
Digested nutrients can no longer pass into the blood

questions.q:
(a) Name the three parts of the secretion of the stomach lining.
(b) Which of the three protects the stomach itself, and from what?
questions.a: (a) Digestive juice, acid and mucus. (b) Mucus; it protects the stomach lining from the acid.
s: Part (b): mucus protects lining from acid

questions.q: Divya's doctor finds that the finger-like projections on the inner lining of her small intestine are damaged. Which activity is most directly reduced?
questions.a: Absorption of digested nutrients into the blood
o: Absorption of digested nutrients into the blood
Churning of food into a semi-liquid mass
Storage of stool until it is expelled
Crushing and chewing of food into pieces

questions.q: Which organ secretes bile, which is mildly basic?
questions.a: The liver

questions.q:
(a) Name the two organs outside the alimentary canal that send secretions into the small intestine.
(b) Both secretions are basic. What does this do to the food coming from the stomach?
questions.a: (a) The liver (bile) and the pancreas (pancreatic juice). (b) Being basic, they neutralise the acids present in the food coming from the stomach.

questions.q: The digestive juice made in the stomach acts mainly on which food component?
questions.a: Proteins

questions.q:
(a) What does the large intestine take from the undigested food?
(b) What is the waste called after this, and where is it kept until it is time to expel it?
questions.a: (a) Water and some salts. (b) Stool; it is stored in the rectum.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The stool becomes semi-solid in the large intestine.
Reason (R): The stool is expelled from the body through the anus.
questions.a: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Seema says: 'Some bacteria in our body are helpful, so every bacterium in our food is helpful too.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. The large intestine has bacteria that help digestion by breaking down undigested food, especially fibre, and making some nutrients, and fermented foods such as curd are good for the digestive system. But it is wrong to say every bacterium is helpful, because some bacteria cause disease.
s: Bacteria in the large intestine help digestion

questions.q:
In a hostel with 40 children, 12 complained of hard stool when breakfast was made of maida. After the warden switched to whole-grain rotis, fruit and vegetables for a month, only 3 still complained. The warden's aim now is to ease the hard stool of these 3, and she can add only one item: a second serving of fruit, or a glass of buttermilk.
(a) Which part of the alimentary canal has the problem, and what in the new breakfast helped it?
(b) Name the process that expels the stool and the part where it waits before that.
(c) What do bacteria in this part do for digestion?
(d) Choose the item for her aim and justify the choice.
questions.a: (a) The large intestine; fibre from whole grains, fruit and vegetables. (b) Egestion through the anus; the stool waits in the rectum. (c) They help digestion by breaking down undigested food, especially fibre, and make some nutrients. (d) A second serving of fruit, as fibre makes the stool easier to pass; buttermilk is good for digestion but fibre addresses the hard stool.
s: Part (d): fruit for the stated aim

questions.q: State three habits for healthy digestion that your book gives along with the Charaka Samhita and modern nutrition.
questions.a: Eating meals at proper times, practising mindful eating, and avoiding overeating.

questions.q: Mohit eats mostly maida biscuits and very few fruits or vegetables and finds the stool hard to pass. Which change is best supported by the book?
questions.a: Add fruits, vegetables and whole grains to his meals
o: Add fruits, vegetables and whole grains to his meals
Chew each bite for fewer seconds
Eat only one very large meal a day
Avoid all foods that contain water

questions.q: Where is the stool stored until the body is ready to expel it?
questions.a: The rectum

questions.q:
The small intestine is about 6 metres long and the large intestine about 1.5 metres.
(a) How many times as long as the large intestine is the small intestine?
(b) Then why is the shorter one called 'large'?
questions.a: (a) 6 / 1.5 = 4 times. (b) The large intestine is wider than the small intestine.

questions.q: Trace the undigested part of a meal from the small intestine to outside the body, naming each stage.
questions.a: It moves into the large intestine, where water and some salts are absorbed to make semi-solid stool. The stool is stored in the rectum and is then expelled through the anus by egestion.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the large intestine.
Statement 1: The stool is stored in the rectum.
Statement 2: The large intestine absorbs water and some salts from the undigested food.
Statement 3: The digestion of proteins is completed in the large intestine.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only

questions.q: The warden of a school hostel plans a day's meals for 30 children. Suggest a fibre-rich food and say how it helps, a fermented food and say how it helps, and two habits for mealtimes from your book.
questions.a: Whole-grain rotis, fruits or vegetables: fibre helps the large intestine function and makes stool easier to pass. Curd or buttermilk: fermented foods are good for the digestive system. Habits: meals at proper times, mindful eating or avoiding overeating.
s: Fibre-rich food with how it helps
Fermented food with how it helps

questions.q: Compare the small intestine and the large intestine on length, width, what each absorbs and what it does with the food, and explain how their names make sense.
questions.a: Small intestine about 6 m, large about 1.5 m. Small is narrower, large is wider. Small intestine absorbs digested nutrients into the blood; large intestine absorbs water and some salts and forms stool. Large is named for width, not length.
s: Water and salts in large intestine, stool

questions.q:
(a) Name two fibre-rich foods from your book.
(b) State the effect of fibre on the large intestine.
questions.a: (a) Any two of fruits, vegetables, whole grains. (b) It helps the large intestine function properly and makes the stool easier to pass.
s: Part (b): helps the large intestine and stool passage

questions.q: Which of these is a fermented food named in your book?
questions.a: Kanji

questions.q: What does the large intestine absorb from the undigested food?
questions.a: Water and some salts

questions.q: Suppose a person's large intestine absorbed almost no water from the undigested food. What would the stool most likely be like?
questions.a: Watery instead of semi-solid
o: Stored in the stomach for longer

questions.q: The expelling of undigested waste through the anus is called
questions.a: egestion

questions.q: Name the ancient text that highlights easily digestible foods and give two spices it mentions for digestion.
questions.a: The Charaka Samhita; ginger, black pepper, cumin (any two).

questions.q:
At a school 'Food Across India' fair, stalls serve kanji, gundruk, curd rice, a fruit salad, fried chips and sweet jalebi. The science club can set up a gut-friendly corner with only two items.
(a) What do kanji, gundruk and curd rice have in common as foods?
(b) In which organ do bacteria live that help digestion, and what do they do?
(c) What does the fruit salad give to the large intestine?
(d) Choose two items that give two different benefits, and justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) They are fermented foods. (b) The large intestine; they break down undigested food, especially fibre, and produce essential nutrients. (c) Fibre, which helps the large intestine function and makes stool easier to pass. (d) Fruit salad (fibre) and kanji or curd rice (fermented food), as together they give both benefits; chips and jalebi give neither.
s: Part (b): large intestine and its bacteria
Part (d): two items with different benefits

questions.q: Name two fermented foods from your book and state one benefit of such foods.
questions.a: Any two of curd, buttermilk, shrikhand, kanji, pickles, gundruk, poita bhat. They are good for a healthy digestive system.

questions.q: Bringing partially digested food back to the mouth for gradual chewing is called
questions.a: rumination

questions.q: Define a ruminant and give two examples.
questions.a: A ruminant is a grass-eating animal that brings partly digested food back to the mouth to chew it thoroughly. Examples: cow, buffalo, goat.

questions.q: A farmer sees his buffalo resting under a tree with its jaws moving steadily, although it is not eating anything. What is the buffalo most likely doing?
questions.a: Chewing partly digested food that came back from its stomach to its mouth
o: Chewing partly digested food that came back from its stomach to its mouth
Breaking the swallowed grass in a gizzard with the help of grit
Absorbing the nutrients of the grass through the walls of its mouth
Producing saliva to clean its teeth between the two daily meals

questions.q: A poultry farmer finds that his hens pick up small stones from the ground. Which is the most reasonable explanation based on the book?
questions.a: The stones help the walls of the gizzard to break the food down
o: The stones help the walls of the gizzard to break the food down
The stones do the work of teeth inside the hen's mouth cavity
The stones are slowly digested and added to the hen's nutrients
The stones neutralise the acid that is made in the hen's stomach

questions.q:
On a dairy farm in Anand the cow Lakshmi chews for about 8 hours a day, even when she is not grazing. The farm also keeps hens. A visitor says, 'Cows and hens both use their stomach to chew food, so they digest the same way.'
(a) Where does the first partial digestion of Lakshmi's grass take place?
(b) After being brought back and chewed, where does the food go?
(c) What does a hen use in place of teeth, and how does it work?
(d) Judge the visitor's statement: what is partly right and what is wrong?
questions.a: (a) In the stomach. (b) It passes down the alimentary canal for further digestion. (c) The gizzard, whose walls contract and relax, often with grit. (d) Partly right: both animals break food down before it goes on for further digestion. Wrong: the cow brings food back to the mouth to chew while the hen's gizzard breaks it by wall movement with grit; hens have no teeth.
s: Part (c): gizzard, wall contraction and relaxation, grit
Part (d): partly right, partly wrong with reasons

questions.q: About how many hours a day does a cow spend chewing its food?
questions.a: 8 hours

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about digestion in ruminants and birds.
Statement 1: In birds, the gizzard sends partly digested food back to the mouth for chewing.
Statement 2: Cows partly digest swallowed grass in the stomach before chewing it again.
Statement 3: The walls of the gizzard contract and relax to break food.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only

questions.q: Differentiate between how a cow and a bird break down food, giving one point each.
questions.a: A cow chews partly digested food again in its mouth after it has been in the stomach. A bird breaks food in its gizzard by wall contractions, often with grit.

questions.q: In which chamber of a bird is food broken down by contraction and relaxation of its walls?
questions.a: The gizzard

questions.q: Ravi says: 'A cow chewing while resting is still digesting, because it is chewing food brought back from its stomach.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. The chewing is rumination. Partly digested food from the stomach is brought back to the mouth and chewed thoroughly, then it passes down for further digestion, so it is part of digestion.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Birds can break down hard grains even though they have no teeth.
Reason (R): The gizzard breaks food by the contraction and relaxation of its walls, often helped by grit.
questions.a: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
A zoo in Mysuru keeps a goat and a peacock. The goat keeps moving its jaws after feeding. The peacock swallows tiny stones with its food. A new keeper wants to feed the peacock only soft hay so that it can 'chew the cud like the goat'.
(a) What structure of the peacock does the work of teeth, and what do the stones do?
(b) What does the goat do with food that has already been swallowed?
(c) Decide whether the keeper's plan suits the peacock and justify using (a) and (b).
questions.a: (a) The gizzard; the stones (grit) help its walls break the food. (b) It brings the partly digested food back to its mouth and chews it again, which is rumination. (c) The plan does not suit: a peacock has no teeth and breaks food in the gizzard with grit rather than re-chewing, and the goat's way is that of a grass-eating ruminant.
s: Part (b): returns food to mouth, rumination

questions.q: Describe the sequence of events in a cow, from swallowing grass to the further digestion, in three steps.
questions.a: The grass is partly chewed and swallowed into the stomach. It is partially digested there and brought back to the mouth for gradual chewing. The thoroughly chewed food passes down the alimentary canal for further digestion.
s: Return to the mouth for chewing

questions.q:
(a) Name the chamber that does the work of teeth in a bird.
(b) Name the material birds swallow to help it and say why they need such a chamber.
questions.a: (a) The gizzard. (b) Grit, small stones; birds have no teeth so the gizzard must break the food.
s: Part (b): grit and absence of teeth

questions.q: Which of the following is a ruminant?
questions.a: Goat

questions.q: Show that a pigeon does not digest food the way a cow does, using what your book says about both.
questions.a: A cow is a grass-eating animal that brings partly digested food from the stomach back to the mouth to chew. A pigeon has no teeth; its food is broken down in the gizzard by contraction and relaxation of its walls, often helped by grit. There is no such returning of food in a bird.
s: Cow returns food to the mouth
Bird has no teeth and uses the gizzard
Gizzard works by wall contraction with grit

questions.q: 'Animals show variations in the alimentary canal.' Justify this using humans, a cow and a bird.
questions.a: In humans teeth crush food in the mouth and the canal runs mouth to anus. A cow partly digests food, returns it to the mouth and chews it again. A bird has no teeth but a gizzard with grit. Different structures suit different ways of digesting different foods.
s: Link between structure and kind of food

questions.q: Which statement about birds is NOT correct?
questions.a: They chew grain with teeth before swallowing
o: They chew grain with teeth before swallowing
They have a chamber called the gizzard
They often swallow grit, small stones
They break food by wall contractions

questions.q: Compare digestion in a cow and in a bird on these points: the breaking up of food, where it happens, what helps it and what the animal swallows.
questions.a: Cow: partly chews, swallows to stomach, partial digestion, brings back and chews gradually in mouth with teeth, about 8 hours a day. Bird: no teeth, food broken in gizzard by contraction and relaxation, helped by swallowed grit. So the two animals break food differently.

questions.q: Differentiate between the chewing of food in a cow and in a human, giving one point each.
questions.a: In a human, teeth chew the food once in the mouth and it is then swallowed for the rest of digestion. In a cow, food is first swallowed, partly digested in the stomach, then brought back to the mouth and chewed gradually.
s: Human: chewed in the mouth and swallowed
Cow: partly digested food returned to the mouth to be chewed

questions.q:
(a) Define rumination.
(b) A cow spends 8 hours a day chewing. How many hours does it spend in one week?
questions.a: (a) Rumination is bringing partly digested food back to the mouth from the stomach and chewing it gradually. (b) 8 x 7 = 56 hours.

questions.q:
A housing society's security guards and some visitors smoke near the gate, inside the compound, close to Imran's block, where his grandfather and baby sister live. The wind carries the smoke to their balcony on most evenings. The society can choose: (i) a smoking corner at the far end of the compound, or (ii) a complete ban inside the compound.
(a) What does the book say smoking releases into the air that puts non-smokers at risk?
(b) Name the term for the harm to Imran's family and the two groups in the family at special risk.
(c) Name, in order, the organs of the respiratory system that the polluted air passes.
(d) Recommend (i) or (ii) and justify it, mentioning one cost of your choice.
questions.a: (a) Toxic chemicals. (b) Passive smoking; a child and an elderly person. (c) Nostrils, nasal passages, windpipe, lungs. (d) A complete ban gives full protection to the family; the cost is that the smokers lose any place to smoke in the compound. A far corner still releases toxic chemicals into the air the wind may carry.
s: Part (b): passive smoking, child and elderly

questions.q: Which is the correct order of the path of inhaled air?
questions.a: Nostrils, nasal passages, windpipe, lungs

questions.q: During inhalation the diaphragm
questions.a: moves down and the ribs move up and outwards
o: moves down and the ribs move up and outwards
moves up and the ribs move down and inwards
moves down and the ribs move down and inwards
moves up and the ribs move up and outwards

questions.q: Describe the pathway of air from the nostrils to the alveoli in three steps.
questions.a: Air enters the nostrils and passes into the nasal passages, where dust is trapped. It goes through the windpipe, which branches into two, one to each lung. The branches divide further and end in alveoli.

questions.q: Tara concludes from Activity 9.3: 'Exhaled air has carbon dioxide but inhaled air has none.' Is her conclusion right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. Lime water in A did not turn milky and in B it did, which shows exhaled air has more carbon dioxide than inhaled air. The test shows 'more', not that inhaled air has none.
s: Evidence from tubes A and B

questions.q: Justify the statement 'Smoking is harmful even to people who do not smoke.'
questions.a: Smoking damages the lungs and raises the risk of lung cancer and other respiratory illnesses; it also causes persistent coughing and frequent infections. It releases toxic chemicals into the air. Non-smokers who inhale this air experience passive smoking, especially dangerous for children, pregnant women and the elderly. So avoiding smoking protects the smoker and others.

questions.q: In the model of Activity 9.2, a student pulls the rubber sheet at the base of the bottle downwards and the balloons inflate. Which statement matches this?
questions.a: It models inhalation, with the diaphragm moving down
o: It models inhalation, with the diaphragm moving down
It models exhalation, with the diaphragm moving up
It models inhalation, with the ribs moving down
It models exhalation, with the lungs pushing the diaphragm

questions.q:
(a) State what happens to the ribs and diaphragm in exhalation.
(b) How does this change the space in the chest and what happens to the air?
questions.a: (a) Ribs move down and inwards; diaphragm moves up. (b) The space reduces and air is pushed out of the lungs.
s: Part (a): ribs down and in, diaphragm up
Part (b): space decreases, air forced out

questions.q: A student working with the model of Activity 9.2 first pushes the rubber sheet up and then pulls it down. Describe what she sees each time, name the action of breathing it stands for, and state what the ribs and diaphragm do in the body in each case.
questions.a: Pushing the sheet up: the balloons deflate; this is exhalation; ribs move down and inwards and the diaphragm moves up, pushing air out. Pulling the sheet down: the balloons inflate; this is inhalation; ribs move up and outwards and the diaphragm moves down, increasing space so air enters. The balloons stand for the lungs and the sheet for the diaphragm.
s: Exhalation with ribs and diaphragm movement
Inhalation with ribs and diaphragm movement

questions.q:
Meera's class repeats Activity 9.3 under the teacher's supervision. Lime water in test tube A gets ordinary air through a pichkari and stays clear. Meera blows through a straw into test tube B and it turns milky. Salim, in a hurry, uses the pichkari again to pass air into his tube C instead of blowing, and the lime water stays clear.
(a) What does the milky colour of tube B show?
(b) Why was tube A included?
(c) Salim says: 'My breath has no carbon dioxide.' Why is his conclusion not supported?
(d) What should the teacher ask him to change before repeating, and what should she check about the lime water?
questions.a: (a) Exhaled air contains more carbon dioxide than inhaled air. (b) To compare with the air we inhale. (c) He tested the same air as tube A (inhaled air), not his breath. (d) Blow through a straw into the lime water; check that the lime water is freshly prepared.
s: Part (a): more carbon dioxide in exhaled air
Part (c): tested inhaled air not breath
Part (d): blow with a straw, fresh lime water

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The rib cage protects the lungs.
Reason (R): On inhalation the ribs move up and outwards.
questions.a: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Why does your book say we should breathe through the nose and not through the mouth?
questions.a: Hair and mucus in the nasal passages trap dust and dirt from the air. Mouth breathing lacks this filtering.
s: So nose breathing keeps the air cleaner

questions.q:
Match each structure in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Nostrils  2. Rib cage  3. Diaphragm  4. Alveoli
Column II: A. protects the lungs  B. dome-shaped muscle that moves down on inhalation  C. balloon-like sacs at the end of the branches in the lungs  D. a pair of openings through which we inhale and exhale
Test tube A has lime water into which ordinary air is passed with a pichkari; test tube B has lime water into which a student blows through a straw. Only B turns milky. What does this show?
questions.a: Exhaled air has more carbon dioxide than inhaled air
o: Exhaled air has more carbon dioxide than inhaled air
Exhaled air has no oxygen in it
Inhaled air has no carbon dioxide at all
The straw added carbon dioxide to the water

questions.q:
In Activity 9.2:
(a) What do the balloons and the rubber sheet represent?
(b) What do the balloons do when the sheet is released upwards, and which action of breathing does this show?
questions.a: (a) Balloons are the lungs; the rubber sheet is the diaphragm. (b) The balloons deflate; it models exhalation.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about breathing and the respiratory system.
Statement 1: Air from the nostrils goes into the lungs without passing through the nasal passages.
Statement 2: The ribs move down and inwards during inhalation.
Statement 3: Lime water turns milky when it reacts with carbon dioxide.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 3 only

questions.q: Define breathing and state how long a person can usually live without it.
questions.a: Breathing is the process of inhaling and exhaling air. Without it we usually cannot survive more than a few minutes.

questions.q: The windpipe branches into smaller branches that end in balloon-like sacs. These sacs are called
questions.a: alveoli

questions.q: What is passive smoking and who may be at special risk?
questions.a: Passive smoking is when non-smokers inhale air polluted by smoke from smokers. Children, pregnant women and the elderly are at special risk.

questions.q: A student writes: 'In one inhalation the ribs move up and outwards while the diaphragm moves up.' Show that this cannot describe a real breath in.
questions.a: In inhalation the chest space must increase so that air enters. Ribs up and outwards increase space but the diaphragm moving up reduces space. Book says in inhalation the diaphragm moves down.

questions.q: Rohit says: 'The lungs only exchange gases; the respiration that releases energy happens inside the body's cells.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. In the lungs oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged at the alveoli (breathing). Respiration, in which oxygen helps break down glucose to release energy, takes place inside the body's cells, and the circulatory system carries oxygen there.
s: Respiration inside the body releasing energy

questions.q:
Priya's science club measures two air samples. Sample P has 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide. Sample Q has 16% oxygen and 5% carbon dioxide. Priya says: 'Only 5 out of 21 is used, so the air in a sealed room can be breathed again and again.'
(a) Which sample is exhaled air?
(b) Which process in the body uses up the oxygen and produces the extra carbon dioxide? Write its word equation.
(c) How does the extra carbon dioxide reach the alveoli?
(d) Evaluate Priya's claim: what is right in it and what is not?
questions.a: (a) Q. (b) Respiration: Glucose + Oxygen gives Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy. (c) The blood carries it to the alveoli. (d) Right: not all the oxygen is used up; 16% remains. Not right: carbon dioxide rises from 0.04% to 5%, about 125 times, so breathing the same air in a sealed room would keep adding carbon dioxide and removing oxygen.
s: Part (d): both parts of the claim judged

questions.q: Which of the following makes up the circulatory system?
questions.a: Heart, blood and blood vessels

questions.q: Which of the following is a chemical process that goes on inside the body?
questions.a: Respiration

questions.q: Nearly what percentage of oxygen does inhaled air contain?
Ravi climbs four floors of stairs and then finds his breathing is faster. Which is the best explanation?
questions.a: His muscles need more energy, which requires more oxygen for respiration
o: His muscles need more energy, which requires more oxygen for respiration
His lungs have become larger because of the climb and take in more air
The air on the upper floors has less oxygen than at ground level
His alveoli directly make energy from the air that he breathes in

questions.q:
(a) Food is broken down to which simple substance that is used in respiration?
(b) What helps to break it down to release energy?
questions.a: (a) Glucose (a simple sugar). (b) Oxygen.

questions.q: Justify: 'Neither food alone nor air alone can give us energy.'
questions.a: Food is broken down to simple substances like glucose, but glucose releases energy only when oxygen helps break it down. Oxygen comes from breathing. So respiration needs both glucose from food and oxygen from air; the circulatory system brings both to the cells. The equation shows both on the left.

questions.q: Using the word equation of respiration, show that exhaled air must contain less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than inhaled air.
questions.a: Respiration uses oxygen and produces carbon dioxide. So oxygen is removed and carbon dioxide added in the body. Therefore exhaled air has less oxygen (16-17% compared with 21%) and more carbon dioxide (4-5% compared with 0.04%).

questions.q: What is the work of the circulatory system?
questions.a: It carries nutrients, oxygen and other substances to all parts of the body and carries waste products away; the heart pumps blood through the blood vessels.

questions.q: A chart gives two air samples. Sample X: oxygen 21%, carbon dioxide 0.04%. Sample Y: oxygen 17%, carbon dioxide 4%. Which is exhaled air and why?
questions.a: Y, because some oxygen was used and carbon dioxide was added in the body
o: Y, because some oxygen was used and carbon dioxide was added in the body
X, because exhaled air carries more oxygen than carbon dioxide in it
Y, because all the oxygen was used up and only carbon dioxide remains
X, because carbon dioxide is not found at all in exhaled air breathed out

questions.q: Trace a molecule of oxygen from the air outside to a muscle cell and say what it does there.
questions.a: It enters through the nostrils, passes through the nasal passages and windpipe to the lungs and alveoli. It passes into the blood, which the circulatory system carries to the muscle cell. There it helps break down glucose to release energy, forming carbon dioxide and water.
s: Respiration in the cell with products

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Exhaled air contains no oxygen at all.
Reason (R): Not all the oxygen we inhale is used up in respiration.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q: Which word equation correctly shows respiration?
questions.a: Glucose + Oxygen gives Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy
o: Glucose + Oxygen gives Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy
Glucose + Carbon dioxide gives Oxygen + Water + Energy
Oxygen + Water gives Glucose + Carbon dioxide + Energy
Glucose + Water gives Oxygen + Carbon dioxide + Energy

questions.q:
Inhaled air has 0.04% carbon dioxide and exhaled air has nearly 4-5%.
(a) By about how many times is the carbon dioxide higher in exhaled air?
(b) How does this extra carbon dioxide reach the alveoli?
questions.a: (a) 4/0.04 = 100 to 5/0.04 = 125 times, about 100 to 125 times. (b) The blood carries it from the body to the alveoli.
s: Part (b): carried by blood to the alveoli

questions.q: Explain how gas exchange takes place in the alveoli.
questions.a: Alveoli have thin walls surrounded by fine blood tubes. Blood brings carbon dioxide from the body, which passes into the alveoli and is exhaled. Oxygen from the alveoli passes into the blood.

questions.q:
(a) Write the word equation of respiration.
(b) Name the two raw materials and say where each comes from.
questions.a: (a) Glucose + Oxygen gives Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy. (b) Glucose, from the digested food; oxygen, from the air we breathe in.
s: Part (b): glucose from food, oxygen from air

questions.q:
At a school sports day, Kabir breathes 18 times a minute at rest and 40 times a minute right after his 100 m race. His friend Dev says, 'Faster breathing just means his lungs are making the energy for the run.'
(a) What is the real source of the energy he used, and what two things are needed for it?
(b) What do the alveoli do during this fast breathing?
(c) Which system carries the oxygen to his leg muscles?
(d) Judge Dev's statement: what is right in it and what is wrong?
questions.a: (a) Respiration of glucose with oxygen; glucose and oxygen are needed. (b) Oxygen passes from the alveoli into the blood and carbon dioxide from the blood passes into the alveoli. (c) The circulatory system. (d) Right: the lungs bring in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide, so faster breathing supports the run. Wrong: energy is released in the body's cells by respiration, not made in the lungs.
s: Part (a): respiration with glucose and oxygen

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about breathing and respiration.
Statement 1: Respiration is a chemical process that goes on inside the body.
Statement 2: Respiration is the inhaling and exhaling of air.
Statement 3: Not all the oxygen we breathe in is used up.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only

questions.q: What does the heart do in the circulatory system, and what does the system carry away from the body's parts?
questions.a: The heart pumps blood through the blood vessels. The system carries waste products away.

questions.q: How does an earthworm obtain oxygen? Why is this a suitable way for its habitat?
questions.a: It exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide through its moist skin. This suits an animal living in moist surroundings, as it needs no lungs or gills.

questions.q: Asha says: 'Every animal uses lungs to breathe because every animal needs oxygen.' Do you agree? Give examples.
questions.a: No. All animals need oxygen but they use different structures. Fish use gills, earthworms use moist skin and frogs use gills as tadpoles and lungs or skin as adults.

questions.q: Show that the statement 'A frog uses only its lungs throughout its life' cannot be right, using what your book says.
questions.a: Tadpoles breathe through gills, so lungs are not used in the early stage. Adult frogs use skin for gas exchange when they stay in water. So the statement fails at two points.

questions.q: Which of the following breathes through its lungs?
questions.a: Lizard

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Fish can take in oxygen from the water they live in.
Reason (R): Their gills are richly supplied with blood vessels and exchange gases between the blood and the gases dissolved in water.
questions.a: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: A pond dries up. Fish lying on the mud gasp and die within minutes, while adult frogs hop away unharmed. Which is the best explanation?
questions.a: Gills work in water, while adult frogs can use their lungs on land
o: Gills work in water, while adult frogs can use their lungs on land
Gills work in air as well as water, but frogs have bigger gills
Fish have lungs that work only in water and frogs have gills
Frogs breathe only through the skin, which does not need water

questions.q:
The eco-club of a school in Kolkata keeps goldfish, tadpoles, adult frogs and earthworms for a display. It has a deep water tank and a land patch with damp soil and a shallow pool. The club must decide where the adult frogs will be kept.
(a) Which breathing organ does the goldfish use?
(b) Which breathing organ does a tadpole use?
(c) How does an adult frog get its oxygen on land and when it stays in water?
(d) Decide whether the adult frogs go in the deep tank or the land patch, and justify it.
questions.a: (a) Gills. (b) Gills. (c) Lungs on land and skin for gas exchange when it stays in water. (d) The land patch with a shallow pool, since the adult frog needs lungs on land and can use skin in water; a deep tank with no land would allow only skin breathing.
s: Part (c): lungs on land, skin in water
Part (d): land patch with pool, reasoned

questions.q: Pooja places an earthworm on a dry, sunny paving stone and it soon stops moving. Which idea best explains this?
questions.a: Its moist skin dries, so gases cannot be exchanged across it
o: Its moist skin dries, so gases cannot be exchanged across it
Its gills dry up in the sun and cannot take up oxygen
Its lungs cannot work in a warm place during the day
Its skin is meant to exchange gases only inside the soil

questions.q: Which of the following does NOT use lungs for breathing?
questions.a: Earthworm

questions.q: Most aquatic animals such as fish breathe through
questions.a: gills

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about breathing in animals.
Statement 1: Tadpoles breathe through gills.
Statement 2: Adult frogs breathe through gills on land and through lungs in water.
Statement 3: Fish exchange gases between their blood and the air through their gills.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 only

questions.q:
(a) Name the breathing organs used by a tadpole and by an adult frog on land.
(b) How does this change help the frog survive on land and in water?
questions.a: (a) Tadpole: gills; adult frog on land: lungs. (b) Lungs on land and skin in water let it live in both places.
s: Part (b): suits both land and water

questions.q: Write a three-clue riddle for an animal that uses gills when young and lungs and skin when adult. Give the answer and say which clue refers to which breathing organ.
questions.a: Clue 1: I breathe through gills when I am young and live in water. Clue 2: When grown up I use lungs on land. Clue 3: In water I exchange gases through my skin. Answer: a frog (tadpole to adult frog).
s: Clues with lungs on land and skin in water

questions.q:
Match each animal in Column I with how it breathes in Column II.
Column I: 1. Lizard  2. Fish  3. Adult frog  4. Earthworm
Column II: A. lungs  B. gills  C. lungs on land and skin in water  D. moist skin

Make a three-column chart in words with the columns 'lungs', 'gills' and 'moist skin'. Place cow, goldfish, adult frog, snake, earthworm and tadpole in it (an animal may go in more than one column), and explain one placement that needed more than one column.
questions.a: Lungs: cow, snake, adult frog (on land). Gills: goldfish, tadpole. Moist skin: earthworm, adult frog (when it stays in water). The adult frog goes in two columns since it uses lungs on land and skin for gas exchange when in water.

questions.q: Describe how a lizard, a fish, a frog (at its different stages) and an earthworm breathe, and explain how each suits its habitat.
questions.a: Lizard: lungs, for land. Fish: gills with blood vessels, exchanging gases dissolved in water. Frog: tadpole gills, adult lungs on land and skin in water, which helps it live on land and in water. Earthworm: moist skin. Different mechanisms suit different habitats.
s: Earthworm moist skin and habitat link

questions.q:
(a) Name the breathing organ of fish and say what it is richly supplied with.
(b) Between what does it exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide?
questions.a: (a) Gills, richly supplied with blood vessels. (b) Between the blood and the gases dissolved in water.
s: Part (b): blood and dissolved gases in water

questions.q:
A zoo is building enclosures for an elephant, a python, a goldfish, an adult frog and an earthworm, but its funds allow only two types of enclosure: a water tank, and a land enclosure with a damp soil patch and a shallow pool.
(a) Which animal needs the water tank, and which breathing organ does it use?
(b) Which animal exchanges gases through its skin all the time, and what must its skin be like?
(c) Place all five animals in the two enclosures, and name the animal that is hardest to place and why.
questions.a: (a) The goldfish; gills. (b) The earthworm; moist skin. (c) Goldfish in the tank; elephant, python and earthworm in the land enclosure (earthworm in the damp soil); adult frog in the land enclosure with its shallow pool. The frog is hardest because it uses lungs on land and skin in water.
s: Part (c): placement and the frog's two needs

questions.q: Differentiate between gills and lungs in terms of the animals that have them and what they exchange gases with.
questions.a: Gills are in most aquatic animals such as fish and exchange gases between blood and gases dissolved in water. Lungs are in animals like birds, cows and snakes and exchange gases with air.
s: Gills: fish, dissolved gases in water

questions.q: Birds, elephants and lions all breathe with lungs. State one way in which their lungs are alike and one way in which they differ.
questions.a: They are alike in being lungs used for breathing in air; the structure of their lungs differs among them.
